fields.Question: How many conics in $\mathbb P^2$ go through 5 generic points?
fields.answer:
You may solve this question by first changing coordinates, and assume 4 of the 5 points are fixed, then solve specific equations, but this is not the right way.

The best method is to look at the collection of conics in $\mathbb P^2$, they are given by equations
\[a_1x^2+a_2y^2+\dots+a_6yz=0\]
up to scaling of $a_1,\dots,a_6$, meaning each conic identify with a point in $\mathbb P^5$. We say $\mathbb P^5$ is a moduli space of conics in $\mathbb P^2$.

With some intersection theory, you can equate passing through 5 points as satisfying 5 general linear equations in $\mathbb P^5$, which gives the answer 1.
fields.Note: Here the conics come with their embeddings in a fixed $\mathbb P^2$. [[Embd|Forgetting the embedding gives a different moduli problem]].

fields.Question: Is there a scheme $\mathcal M$ such that maps $X\to\mathcal M$ correspond naturally to isomorphism classes of line bundles on $X$?
fields.answer:
Suppose there is. Take $X=\mathbb P^1$ and let $f_0,f_1:\mathbb P^1\to\mathcal M$ correspond to $\mathcal O$ and $\mathcal O(1)$.

Cover $\mathbb P^1$ by its two usual affine charts $U_0,U_1\cong\mathbb A^1$. Both line bundles restrict to the trivial line bundle on either chart:
$$\mathcal O|_{U_j}\cong\mathcal O(1)|_{U_j}\cong\mathcal O_{U_j}.$$
By naturality, $f_0|_{U_j}=f_1|_{U_j}$ for $j=0,1$. Since morphisms of schemes are determined locally, we get $f_0=f_1$. This would imply $\mathcal O\cong\mathcal O(1)$, which is false: their degrees are $0$ and $1$.

So the functor of isomorphism classes of line bundles cannot be represented by a scheme.
fields.Note: What went wrong? We kept the fact that the bundles are locally isomorphic, but lost the isomorphisms used to compare and glue them. [[Stki|Remembering those isomorphisms]] leads us toward stacks.

fields.definition:
$f:X\to Y$ is $\emph{quasi-finite}$ if for all $y\in Y$ the fiber 
\[X_y:=X\times_Y\mathrm{Spec}k(y)\]
is finite.

it is $\emph{locally quasi-finite}$ if for all $x\in X$ there exists $x\in U$ open such that $f|_U$ is quasi-finite.

fields.text:
The map 
$$\coprod_{i=1}^\infty\mathrm{Spec}k\to\mathrm{Spec}k$$
is locally quasi-finite but not quasi-finite.

fields.statement: $f:X\to Y$ is $\'\text{e}$tale if and only if it is smooth and [[70882560-8548-4ef5-9294-b7e097aa32dc|locally quasi-finite]].

$f:X\to Y$ is $\'\text{e}$tale if and only if for all $x\in X$,there exists $x\in U$ open affine, such that, there exists $V\subseteq Y$ open affine with $f(U)\subseteq V$ such that $f|_U$ is standard etale.

fields.definition:
$\mathrm{\'et}(X)$ is the site where 
\begin{itemize}
\item objects are $\'\text{e}$tale morphisms $Y\to X$
\item morphisms are morphisms over $X$ (necessarily $\'\text{e}$tale).
\end{itemize}
$\mathrm{Cov}(Y\to X)$ consists of 
\[\{Y_i\to Y\}_{i\in I}\]
such that $\coprod_i Y_i\to Y$ is surjective.

fields.text:
Consider $\mathrm{\'et}(\mathrm{Spec}K)$.
The objects are $\coprod \mathrm{Spec}L_i\to \mathrm{Spec} K$ for $L_i$ finite and separable.
Therefore $\mathrm{Spec} \mathbb Q(\sqrt 2)\to \mathrm{Spec}\mathbb Q$ is a covering.

fields.definition:
$\mathrm{\'Et}(X)$ is the site of category $\mathrm{Sch}_X$ where
$\mathrm{Cov}(Y\to X)$ consists of 
\[\{Y_i\xrightarrow{\mathrm{\'et}} Y\}_{i\in I}\]
such that $\coprod_i Y_i\to Y$ is surjective.
A $\emph{topos}$ $T$ is a category equivalent to sheaves on a site.

fields.text:
For each scheme $X$, keep a category whose objects are line bundles on $X$ and whose morphisms are isomorphisms of line bundles.

Now two objects can be isomorphic without being equal, and the isomorphism itself is part of the data. When we glue local line bundles, the chosen isomorphisms on overlaps must be remembered and must agree on triple overlaps.

A scheme gives a set $\operatorname{Hom}(X,\mathcal M)$. For a stack, the corresponding collection has the structure of a category, so it can retain these isomorphisms. This is the motivation for thinking of stacks as a generalization of sheaves using categories.

cards.title: Example (Projective space and line bundles with sections)

fields.Question: Why does the line bundle example not contradict the fact that $\mathbb P^n$ is a scheme?
fields.answer:
A map $f:X\to\mathbb P^n$ remembers more than a line bundle. It gives
$$L=f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^n}(1)$$
together with the pulled-back coordinate sections $s_0,\ldots,s_n\in\Gamma(X,L)$, which generate $L$ everywhere.

Conversely, a line bundle $L$ with $n+1$ generating sections defines a map to $\mathbb P^n$. On the open set where $s_i$ generates $L$, its coordinates are the regular functions $s_j/s_i$. These local maps agree on overlaps.

Thus maps to $\mathbb P^n$ correspond to isomorphism classes of pairs $(L,(s_0,\ldots,s_n))$ with
$$\mathcal O_X^{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow L.$$
An isomorphism of pairs must carry each $s_i$ to the corresponding section.
fields.Note: The sections have no common zero. Forgetting them leaves the [[a37887f5-925c-4820-9fa2-50ef14b20d11|moduli problem of line bundles]], which is not represented by a scheme.

fields.text:
The [[a6fda3d0-9c7a-4775-9331-53d618f5c6e0|space $\mathbb P^5$ of conics]] classifies conics inside a fixed $\mathbb P^2$. We remember the inclusion $i:C\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^2$, not just the abstract curve $C$.

The embedding gives the line bundle $i^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^2}(1)$ and the three pulled-back coordinate sections. This is the extra data in the [[Lsec|projective-space interpretation]].

An automorphism $\varphi:C\to C$ compatible with the fixed embedding satisfies $i\circ\varphi=i$, and therefore $\varphi=\mathrm{id}_C$. Abstract curves can have nontrivial automorphisms; forgetting the embedding changes the problem.

fields.definition:
A presheaf $\mathcal F$ consists of a set $\mathcal F(U)$ for each open subset $U\subseteq X$, and a restriction map
$$\rho_U^V:\mathcal F(V)\to\mathcal F(U)$$
for every inclusion $U\subseteq V$.

These maps satisfy
$$\rho_W^V\circ\rho_V^U=\rho_W^U\quad(W\subseteq V\subseteq U),\qquad\rho_U^U=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal F(U)}.$$
So restricting in stages is the same as restricting directly, and restricting to the same open set does nothing.
fields.Note:
Let $\mathrm{Open}_X$ be the category of open subsets of $X$, with inclusions as morphisms. The same data form a functor
$$\mathcal F:\mathrm{Open}_X^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Sets}.$$

fields.definition:
A presheaf on $\mathcal C$ is a functor
$$\mathcal F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathrm{Sets}.$$
fields.Example:
[[Psht|Presheaves on a topological space]] use $\mathcal C=\mathrm{Open}_X$.
[[Repr|Representable presheaves]] are another basic example.

fields.definition: The objects of $\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C)$ are [[Pshc|presheaves on $\mathcal C$]]. A morphism $\eta:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ is a natural transformation.

fields.setting: $\mathcal C$ is locally small. Fix $X\in\mathcal C$.
fields.definition:
The presheaf represented by $X$ is
$$h_X(Y)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(Y,X).$$
For $u:Y'\to Y$, restriction is precomposition:
$$h_X(u):h_X(Y)\to h_X(Y'),\qquad g\mapsto g\circ u.$$
A presheaf $\mathcal F$ is representable if it is isomorphic to some $h_X$.
fields.Note: The set $h_X(Y)$ describes $X$ as seen by maps from the test object $Y$. The [[Yond|Yoneda embedding]] says that remembering all these sets and restriction maps retains the data of $\mathcal C$.

fields.statement:
There is a fully faithful functor
$$\mathcal C\longrightarrow\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C),\qquad X\longmapsto h_X.$$
A morphism $f:X\to Y$ induces the natural transformation whose component at $T$ sends $g:T\to X$ to $f\circ g:T\to Y$. In particular,
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{Pre}(\mathcal C)}(h_X,h_Y).$$
fields.proof:
Given a natural transformation $\eta:h_X\to h_Y$, recover the morphism
$$f=\eta_X(\mathrm{id}_X):X\to Y.$$
Naturality then forces $\eta_T(g)=f\circ g$ for every $g:T\to X$. Thus every natural transformation comes from exactly one morphism.

fields.text:
Let $L/K$ be a Galois extension with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)=G$. 
Let $\mathcal{F}\in \mathrm{sh}(\mathrm{\'et}(\mathrm{Spec}K))$, then $G$ acting on $\mathrm{Spec}L$ gives an action on $\mathcal{F}(L)$. 
The sheaf axiom then tells us 
\[\mathcal{F}(K)\to \mathcal{F}(L)\to \mathcal{F}(L\otimes_KL)\]
is an equalizer.

If $L=K(\alpha)$ with minimal polynomial $f$, then 
\[L\otimes_KL=L\otimes_KK[x]/(f(x))=L[x]/(f(x))\]
Since $L$ is a Galois extension, $f(x)$ splits into $\prod_{g\in G} (x-g\alpha)$
and the right hand side becomes $\bigoplus_{g\in G}L$.
The two maps of 
\[L\to L\otimes_KL\cong\bigoplus_{g\in G} L\]
then becomes $x\mapsto x$ and $x\mapsto gx$.

Hence $\mathcal{F}(K)$ can be described as elements of $\mathcal{F}(L)$ that restrict equality via the two maps, meaning $G$-invariant sections in $\mathcal{F}(L)$
\[\mathcal{F}(K)=\mathcal{F}(L)^G\]
fields.Remark: The higher cohomology of $\mathcal{F}$ here gives Galois cohomology.

fields.text:
As \'etale maps are comparable to covering spaces, we in fact have a notion of \'etale fundamental group, which when applied to complex manifolds, is a profinite completion of the usual fundamental group
\[\pi_1^{\mathrm{\'et}}(X)=\widehat{\pi_1(X)}\]

fields.definition:
A \emph{morphism of topoi} 
\[f:T'\to T\]
is a triple $(f^*,f_*,\phi)$
such that 
\[\phi:\mathrm{Hom}(f^*(-),-)\to \mathrm{Hom}(-,f_*(-))\]
is an equivalence and $f^*$ commutes with finite limits.

A \emph{continuous} map of sites 
\[f:\mathcal{C}\to \mathcal{C'}\]
is a function of categories such that if
\[\{X_i\to X\}_{i\in I}\in\mathrm{Cov}(X)\]
then 
\[\{f(X_i)\to f(X)\}_{i\in I}\in\mathrm{Cov}(X).\]
fields.Examples:
[[VKTM|Example (Continuous map of site 1)]]
[[TLSN|Example (Continuous map of site 2)]]

fields.text:
If $f:X\to Y$ is a continuous map of topological spaces, then 
\[f^{-1}:\mathrm{Open}_Y\to \mathrm{Open}_X\]
is a continuous map of sites.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a map of schemes, then since pullbacks of \'etale surjective are \'etale surjective, it induces a continuous map 
\[\mathrm{\'et}(Y)\to \mathrm{\'et}(X).\]

fields.statement: We have an induced map of topoi $T\to T'$.

fields.text:
Consider the [[Yond|Yoneda embedding]]
\[\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow \widehat{\mathcal{C}}.\]
For a continuous map 
\[f:\mathcal{C}'\to \mathcal{C}\]
we can set
\[f^*(h^a_{X'}=h^a(f(X')\]
Then
\begin{align}
\mathrm{Hom}(f^*(h^a_{X'}),\mathcal{F})=&\mathrm{Hom}(h^a_{X'},f_*\mathcal{F})\\
=&\mathrm{Hom}(h_{X'},f_*\mathcal{F})\\
=&f_*\mathcal{F}(X')=\mathcal{F}(f(X'))\\
=&\mathrm{Hom}(h^a_{f(X')},\mathcal{F})
\end{align}
Hence $h^a_{f(X')}=f^*(h^a_{X'})$.

fields.Settings:
If $f:X\to Y$ is \emph{faithfully [[98fbf737-0192-48dc-a4a6-9873c0635a16|flat]]} if it is flat and surjective.
$f$ is \emph{fppf} if $f$ is locally of finite presentation and faithfully flat.
fields.definition:
The \emph{fppf site} is 
\[\mathcal{C}=\mathrm{Sch}_{X}\]
with 
\[\mathrm{Cov}(Y\to X)\]
consisting of $\{Y_i\to Y\}$ flat and locally of finite presentation such that 
\[\coprod Y_i\to Y\]
is surjective.
fields.Remark:
Since open immersions are \'etale, which are flat and locally of finite presentation, we have maps of topoi
\[X_{\mathrm{fppf}}\to X_{\mathrm{\'et}}\to X_{\mathrm{Zar}}.\]
fields.Motivation: [[AEJO|fppf descent]]: typically most properties are stable under base change along fppf cover (and conversely).

fields.statement:
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $M$ is flat and 
\[\mathrm{Hom}_R(N,N')\to\mathrm{Hom}_R(N\otimes M,N'\otimes M) \]
is injective.
\item $M$ is flat and for all $N$,
\[N\to \mathrm{Hom}(M,N'\otimes M)\]
\[y\mapsto (m\mapsto y\otimes m)\]
is injective.
\item $M$ is [[ULJD|faithfully flat]].
\item $N'\to N$ is injective iff 
\[N'\otimes M\to N\otimes M\]
is injective.
\item $M$ is flat and $N\otimes M=0$ implies $N=0$.
\item $M$ is flat and for all $\mathfrak{m}\subseteq R$ maximal, $M/\mathfrak{m}M\neq 0$.
\item Same as (6) but replace max by prime.
\end{enumerate}

fields.text: The whole point of flatness if so we can preserve cohomology when tensoring.

fields.statement: $\mathrm{Spec}B\to \mathrm{Spec} A$ is faithfully flat if and only if $B$ is faithfully flat as an $A$ module.
fields.proof: For surjectivity, let $\mathrm{Spec} A/\mathfrak p\to \mathrm{Spec}A$ be a point, the taking fiber product gives a point $\mathrm{Spec} B/\mathfrak p B\to \mathrm{Spec}B$, and we have surjective iff $B/\mathfrak pB\neq 0$.

fields.hypotheses: $f:X \to Y$ flat, and locally of finite presentation
fields.statement: $f$ is open.
fields.Proof: Use [[ENAC|Theorem (Chevalley's Theorem)]] and [[LVZJ|Lemma (Constructible)]]. Suppose $U$ is open, need to show $f(U)$ is stable under generalization. Assume $X,Y$ local with $\mathrm{Spec}B\to \mathrm{Spec}A$ flat. Start with point $\mathfrak{p}$, want unique maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ that lifts to maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}'$. Going down tells us we have $\mathfrak{p}'$.

fields.hypotheses: $f:X\to Y$ is locally of finite presentation
fields.statement: $f$ sends constructible set to constructible.

fields.hypotheses: $E\subseteq Y$ is constructible and stable under generalization/specialization.
fields.statement: then $E$ is open/closed, respectively.

fields.hypotheses:
$X\to Y$ is fppf.
$U\subseteq Y$ is open and quasi-compact (e.g. affine).
fields.statement:
\[f^{-1}(U)=\bigcup_jV_j\]
with $V_j$ quasi-compact andeach $f(V_j)=U$.
fields.Note: This property is called \emph{fpqc}, so this says fppf implies fpqc.
fields.Proof:
Enough to show for every $x\in f^{-1}(U)$, there exists [[VPTI|open]] quasi-compact neighbourhood $V$ such that $f(V)=U$.

Choose open affine cover 
\[f^{-1}(U)=\bigcup W_i.\]
$f$ is flat surjective so $f(W_i)$ open and cover $U$. Since $U$ is quasi-compact, choose finite subcover and throw in a neighbourhood around $x$.

fields.definition:
A property $\mathcal{P}$ is \emph{$\tau$-local on the base} if for all squares
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{X'} & X \\
	{S'} & S
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{f'}", from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["f"', from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\tau\text{-covering}}", from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
$f$ has $\mathcal{P}$ iff $f'$ does.

$\mathcal{P}$ is \emph{$\tau$-local on the source} if 
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{X'} & X \\
	& S
	\arrow["{\tau\text{-covering}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{f'}"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["f", from=1-2, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
$f'$ has $\mathcal{P}$ if $f$ does.

fields.text: Smooth is Zariski-local on the source.

fields.Proof:
Universally closed (which implies a bunch of others):
Need to show
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{X_T} & X \\
	T & S
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\text{closed?}}", from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["f", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\forall", from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
Have $f'$ universally closed, and want $g$ closed.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{X'_{T'}} && {X_T} & \\
	& {X'} && X \\
	{T'} && T \\
	& {S'} && S
	\arrow["{\pi'}"', from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{g'}"', from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow["g", from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-4]
	\arrow["{f'}"{pos=0.8}, from=2-2, to=4-2]
	\arrow["f", from=2-4, to=4-4]
	\arrow["\pi"'{pos=0.8}, from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=4-2]
	\arrow[from=3-3, to=4-4]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=4-4]
\end{tikzcd}\]
Since $f'$ is universally closed, $g'$ is closed. 
Since $\pi$ is fppf, $\pi'$ is fppf, so both are [[VPTI|open]] and surjective.
Thus for all $W\subseteq T$, $W$ is closed iff $\pi^{-1}(W)$ is cloed. 
Let $Z\subseteq X_T$ be closed. Want $g(Z)$ closed. So apply $(\pi')^{-1}, g',\pi$.

fields.statement:
$h_X$ is [[PDHD|a sheaf]] in the [[KDLS|fppf site]], i.e.
For fppf cover $\{Y_i\to Y\}$, 
\[h_X(Y)\to \prod_ih_x(Y_i)\to\prod h_X(Y_i\times_YY_j)\]
is exact. Eequivalently,
if $Y$ is covered by $Y_i$ and we look at fiber products $Y_{ij}$. Morphisms $Y_i\to X$ compatible with restriction will glue.

fields.text:
If $\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf and $L/K$ has [[UQIU|Galois group]] $G$, then
\[\mathcal{F}(K)=\mathcal{F}(L)^G.\]
For $\mathcal{F}=h_X$, we have $\mathrm{Spec}(K)\to X$ is equivalent to $G$-equivariant $\mathrm{Spec}L\to X$.

fields.hypotheses: $A\to B$ is faithfully flat, and $M$ is an $A$-module.
fields.statement:
The following is exact,
\[M\xrightarrow{f}M\otimes_AB\xrightarrow{p_1,p_2}M\otimes B\otimes B\]
where $p_1:m\otimes b\mapsto m\otimes b\otimes 1$ and $p_1:m\otimes b\mapsto m\otimes 1\otimes b$.
fields.Proof:
We need 
\[0\to M\to M\otimes B\xrightarrow{p_1-p_2} M\otimes B\otimes B\]
to be exact.
By [[SXWW|faithful flatness]], we can tensor $B$ and show exact.
\[M\xrightarrow{f'}M\otimes_AB\xrightarrow{p_1',p_2'}M\otimes B\otimes B\]
The advantage for this complication is that we now have a section:
Define 
\[M\otimes B\otimes B\xrightarrow{\tau}M\otimes_AB\xrightarrow{\gamma}M\]
where $\gamma:m\otimes b\otimes b'\mapsto m\otimes bb'$ and $\tau: m\otimes b\otimes b'\otimes b''\to m\otimes b\otimes b'b''$.
This immediately gives $f'$ injective because it has section, and $\tau p_1'=\mathrm{id}, \tau p_2'=f'\gamma$. 
Exactness in the middle: for $\alpha\in M\otimes B \otimes B$ such that $p_1'(\alpha)=p_2'(\alpha)$, 
\[\alpha=\tau p_1'(\alpha)=\tau p_2'(\alpha)=f'(\gamma(\alpha)),\] 
so exact.

fields.statement:
If $U,V,X$ affine, and $V\to U$ is fppf cover, then 
\[h_X(U)\to h_X(V)\to h_X(V\times V)\]
is exact.

$\mathcal{F}$ is an fppf sheaf if and only if for all fppf cover $V\to U$, 
\[\mathcal{F}(U\to \mathcal{F}(V)\to \mathcal{F}(V\times V)\]
is exact (only need to check on singleton covers).
fields.Proof:
Start with any fppf cover $\{U_i\to U\}$. Let $V=\coprod U_i$.
Have map 
\[\mathcal{F}(V)\to \prod_i\mathcal{F}(U_i)\]
which is an isomorphism since $\mathcal{F}$ is a big Zariski sheaf.

fields.statement:
$\mathcal{F}$ is fppf sheaf if and only if for all fppf cover $V\to U$ with $V,U$ affine 
\[\mathcal{F}(U)\to \mathcal{F}(V)\to \mathcal{F}(V\times V)\]
exact.
fields.proof:
By the [[ZSEY|previous lemma]], just need to check sheaf axiom on fppf $V\to U$ where $V,U$ are not necessarily affine. We want $\mathcal{F}(U)\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F}(V)$.
Let $U=\cup_i U_i$ with $f^{-1}(U_i)=\bigcup V_{ij}$ by affines. By affine case,
\[\mathcal{F}(U)\to \prod \mathcal{F}(U_i),\quad \mathcal{F}(V)\to \prod\mathcal{F}(V_{ij})\]
are injective. Need 
\[\prod \mathcal{F}(U_i)\to \prod\mathcal{F}(V_{ij})\]
injective. Since [[VPTI|$f$ is open]], $U_i=\bigcup f(V_{ij})$. Since $U_i$ affine, it is quasi-compact and has finite subcover, so $U_i=\bigcup V_{i,j_k}$. 
Then $\coprod V_{i,j_k}\to U_i$ is a fppf cover by affine, and 
\[\prod \mathcal{F}(U_i)\hookrightarrow \prod\mathcal{F}(V_{i,j_k})\hookrightarrow \prod\mathcal{F}(V_{i,j}).\]

Exactness in middle: reduce to $U$ affine. Then diagram chase. Then reduce to $V$ quasi compact. Then reduce to both $U,V$ affine.

fields.definition: A \emph{fibered category} over $\mathcal{C}$ is a category $\mathcal{F}$ and a functor $p:\mathcal{F}\to \mathcal C$ such that pullbacks exist.

A morphism $\phi:U\to V$ in a [[CXRR|fibered category]] $\mathcal F$ is \emph{Cartesian} if
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	W && \\
	{p(W)} & U & V \\
	& {p(U)} & {p(V)}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["{\exists ! \lambda}"{description}, dashed, from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\forall \psi}", from=1-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow["{\forall h}"', from=2-1, to=3-2]
	\arrow["{p(\psi)}"{description}, from=2-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\phi", from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow["{p(\phi)}"', from=3-2, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}\]
exists uniuqe $\lambda$ such that $p(\lambda)=h$.

We will say $U$ is a \emph{pullback} of $V$ along $p(\phi)$.

Given $p:\mathcal F\to \mathcal C$, for all $U\in \mathcal C$, let $\mathcal{F}(U)$ be the category where 
objects are $X\in \mathcal F$ such that $p(X)=U$.
morphisms are $\phi:X\to Y$ such that $p(\phi)=\mathrm{id}_U$.

fields.text:
Let $\mathcal M_g\to \mathrm{Sch}$, where family of curves over $X$ is mapped to $X$.
Objects are $f:C\to X$ [[98fbf737-0192-48dc-a4a6-9873c0635a16|flat maps]]. Morphisms need to form commutative diagram. Pullbacks are cartesian squares.

Let $\mathcal M_{g,n}\to \mathrm{Sch}$. Marked points are given by sections of $f:C\to X$. Morphisms need to send (ordered) marked points to (ordered) marked points.

$\mathcal{M}_{1,1}$ is upperhalf plane mod $SL_2(\mathbb Z)$.
$\mathcal{Qcoh}\to Sch$ is a fibered category sending $(X,\mathcal{Q})$ to $X$. Morphisms are maps $h^*\mathcal{Q}\to \mathcal{Q}'$, so $\mathcal{Qcoh}(X)=\mathrm{Qcoh}(X)$.
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be any category, $X\in \mathcal{C}$. Then $\mathcal{C}/X$ with objects $Y\to X$ is a fibered category.

fields.definition: Let $p_{\mathcal{F}},p_{\mathcal G}$ be fibered category over $\mathcal{C}$, then $p_{\mathcal{F}}\to p_{\mathcal G}$ is a functor $g:\mathcal{F}\to \mathcal{G}$ that sends [[ZWGG|Cartesian arrow]] to Cartesian arrow.

fields.text:
$\mathcal{M}_{g,1}\to \mathcal{Qcoh}$ sending $(C,s)$ to $s^*\Omega_{C/X}^1$ is a morphism of fibered category because $g^*\Omega^1_{C/X}=\Omega_1^{C'/X'}$ which gives
\[h^*s^*\Omega^1_{C/X}=s'g^*\Omega^1_{C/X}=(s')^*\Omega^1_{C/X}\]
so [[ZWGG|Cartesian arrows]] are sent to Cartesian arrows.

fields.definition: Let $g,g'$ be [[ZKIP|morphisms of fibered categories]]. Then a \emph{base-preserving natural transformation} $\alpha:g\to g'$ is a natural transformation of functors such that for all $U\in\mathcal{F}$, $\alpha_U$ satisfies $p_{\mathcal{F}}(\alpha_U)=\mathrm{id}_{p_{\mathcal{G}}(U)}$, i.e. $\alpha_U$ is a morphism in $\mathcal{F}(p_{\mathcal{F}}(U))$.
fields.Remark: If we denote maps between fibered categories form a category $\mathrm{HOM}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G})$, whose morphisms are base-preserving.

fields.definition:
Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a site and $\mathcal{F}$ a [[Pshc|presheaf]] on $\mathcal{C}$. Then $\mathcal{F}$ is a \textbf{sheaf} if for all $\{U_i\to U\}_{i\in I}\in \mathrm{Cov}(U)$, the diagram
		\[
			\begin{tikzcd}
				\mathcal{F}(U)\ar[r] & \prod_{i\in I} \mathcal{F}(U_i)\ar[r, shift left=0.75]\ar[r, shift right=0.75] & \prod_{i,j\in I}\mathcal{F}(U_i\cap U_j)
			\end{tikzcd}
		\]
is an equalizer.

fields.definition:
A morphism $X\to Y$ of schemes is \textbf{formally smooth} if for any ring $A$ and any nilpotent ideal $I\subset A$ with a commutative diagram
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					\mathrm{Spec}(A/I)\ar[d, hook]\ar[r] & X\ar[d]\\
					\mathrm{Spec}(A) \ar[r]\ar[ur, dashed, "\exists"] & Y
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
the diagonal morphism exists.

A morphism $X\to Y$ of schemes is \textbf{formally \'etale} if for any ring $A$ and any nilpotent ideal $I\subset A$ with a commutative diagram
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					\mathrm{Spec}(A/I)\ar[d, hook]\ar[r] & X\ar[d]\\
					\mathrm{Spec}(A) \ar[r]\ar[ur, dashed, "\exists !"] & Y
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
the diagonal morphism exists and is unique.

fields.text:
Let $Y=\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}$ and $A=\mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ and $I=(\varepsilon)$ (here there's no need to put $\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}$ at the bottom since everything has a unique arrow to it). We have the diagram	
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}\ar[r]\ar[d, hook] & X\\
					\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2 \ar[ur, dashed, swap, "\exists\text{ or }\exists !"] &
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
A map $\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}\to X$ corresponds to choosing $x\in X(\mathbb{C})$ and $h:\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2\to X$ is a choice of $x+\varepsilon y\in X(\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon^2=0$, i.e., a tangent vector. So formal smoothness means we can ''thicken'' every point to a tangent vector. In particular, we can keep extending:
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}\ar[r]\ar[d, hook] & X\\
					\mathrm{Spec}\ \mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2\ar[d, hook] \ar[ur, dashed, swap] & \\
					\mathrm{Spec} \mathbb{C}[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^3 \ar[uur, bend right, dashed]\ar[d, hook] & \\
					\vdots
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
so we get first order information, second order information, etc at each step. In particular, for such schemes, we can apply Hensel's lemma to obtain ``approximate roots''.

cards.title: Example (The squaring map is not formally smooth)

fields.text:
The following is an example of a morphism which is \textbf{not} formally smooth. Take $X=\mathbb{A}^1_k=Y$ with $k$ algebraically closed and of characteristic 0, and consider the morphism $\phi:X\to Y$, $x\mapsto x^2$. The corresponding map of rings $\phi^\#:k[y]\to k[x]$ (where $x,y$ are the coordinates on $X,Y$ respectively) is given by $y\mapsto x^2$. We claim $\phi$ is not formally smooth.  Consider $A=k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ and $I=(\varepsilon)$ with the diagram
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					\mathrm{Spec}\ k\ar[r, "0"]\ar[d, hook] & \mathbb{A}^1\ar[d, "\phi"]\\
					\mathrm{Spec}\ k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2 \ar[r]& \mathbb{A}^1
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
where $\mathrm{Spec}\ k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2\to \mathbb{A}^1$ is given by $\varepsilon\mapsto 0$, i.e., $k[y]\ni y\mapsto \varepsilon\in  k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$.
Equivalently,
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					 k & k[x]\ar[l, swap, "0"]\\
					 k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2 \ar[u,two heads] & k[y]\ar[l]\ar[u,hook,swap, "\phi^\#"]
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
We want to make sure there is no diagonal homomorphism $\psi:k[x]\to k[\varepsilon]/\varepsilon^2$ making the diagram commute. If such a homomorphism $\psi$ existed, then looking at the lower right triangle gives $\varepsilon=\psi\phi^\#(y)=\psi(x^2)=\psi(x)^2$. However, $\varepsilon$ has no square root, so no such map can exist.

This example fails to be formally smooth because it is ramified at zero. Indeed, since $\phi^\#_{0}:\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^1,0}=k[y]_{(y)}\to \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{A}^1,\phi(0)}=k[x]_{(x)}$ is determined by $\phi^\#(x)=x^2$, we have
		\[
			\phi^\#_{(x)}((y))=x^2k[x]_{(x)}\neq xk[x]_{(x)}.
		\]

fields.definition:
A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is \textbf{smooth} (resp. \textbf{\'etale}) if it is [[CIEH|formally smooth]] (resp, [[VFRH|formally étale]]) and is locally of finite presentation, i.e., for all $x\in X$, there exists $U\ni x$ and $V\ni f(x)$ with $U=\mathrm{Spec}\ A$, $V=\mathrm{Spec}\ B$ such that $f(U)\subset V$ and
			\[
				A=B[x_1,\dots, x_n]/(f_1,\dots, f_r).
			\]

fields.text:
Let $\mathcal{M}_g$ be the moduli stack of genus $g$ curves. A morphism $T\to \mathcal{M}_g$ corresponds to a morphism $C\to T$ [[98fbf737-0192-48dc-a4a6-9873c0635a16|flat]] and locally of finite presentation such that [[USTA|all fibres are genus $g$ curves]]. [[CIEH|Formal smoothness]] is then a lifting problem
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					T=\mathrm{Spec} A/I \ar[r]\ar[d,hook] & \mathcal{M}_g\\
					T'=\mathrm{Spec} A\ar[ur, dashed, swap, "\exists"] & 
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
which corresponds to a pullback diagram
			\[
				\begin{tikzcd}
					C\ar[r, dashed] \ar[d] & C' \ar[d, dashed]\\
					T\ar[r, hook] & T'
				\end{tikzcd}
			\]
This can thus be seen as a deformation theory problem.
